news_summary: Advancements in frozen fiber technology significantly enhance the interaction between light and sound, boosting their coupling strength by 1,000 times.
news_summary_fr: Les progrès réalisés dans le domaine de la technologie des fibres congelées améliorent considérablement l'interaction entre la lumière et le son, multipliant par 1 000 la force de leur couplage.
news_summary_es: Los avances en la tecnología de fibra congelada mejoran significativamente la interacción entre la luz y el sonido, multiplicando por 1.000 la intensidad de su acoplamiento.

articles.title: This frozen fiber makes light and sound interact 1,000x more strongly
articles.summary: Freezing the liquid core of an optical fiber produced an extreme environment where light and sound interact more than 1,000 times more strongly than in ordinary fibers. Researchers used the effect to create optoacoustic memory, potentially paving the way for lower-energy photonic computers and advanced quantum technologies.
articles.content:
The transformation of a liquid into a solid is familiar in nature. Lava flowing from a volcano eventually cools and hardens into rock, while water in a lake can freeze into ice during a cold winter. When materials undergo these phase changes, important physical properties can change as well, including density and refractive index, which affect how sound and light travel through them.

A related process plays an important role in manufacturing optical fibers. Glass preforms are heated until their structure becomes loose enough to be drawn into extremely thin fibers. Light travels through the fiber core, allowing information to move rapidly across long distances. This ability has made optical fibers essential to modern telecommunications.

Scientists have also developed specialized optical fibers for technologies including fiber lasers, fiber endoscopes, and fiber sensors. Some hollow core fibers can be filled with gases or liquids, allowing them to map temperature distributions or even function as tiny laboratories for chemical experiments.

Freezing a Liquid Core at Extreme Temperatures

Researchers from the Max Planck Institute of the Science of Light (MPL) in Erlangen, the Leibniz University Hannover (LUH) and the Leibniz Institute for Photonic Technologies (IPHT) in Jena have now taken liquid core optical fibers (LiCOF) in a new direction.

The team cooled the liquid inside the fibers with nitrogen at -196 °C, causing the material in the core to change from a liquid into a solid. Surprisingly, freezing the core did not prevent the fiber from carrying light.

"The key point is, that the frozen section of the LiCOF retains its ability to guide light. Not only that, but both the liquid and the frozen section of the fiber also guide hypersonic sound waves," says Simon Seiderer, one of the three lead authors of the article and a researcher in the "Quantum Optoacoustics" research group of Prof. Dr. Birgit Stiller, who leads the project.

Light and Sound Interact More Than 1,000 Times More Strongly

The researchers took advantage of the unusually strong interaction between light and sound inside the frozen fiber. This phenomenon, called Brillouin-Mandelstam scattering, is already known from conventional optical fibers.

Freezing the liquid core, however, creates an exceptionally dense and tightly confined environment. Under these conditions, the interaction between light and sound becomes more than 1000 times stronger than it is in standard optical fibers.

That dramatic increase allowed the team to demonstrate optoacoustic memory, a key component that could be used in photonic neuromorphic computing inside fibers.

The approach relies on the enormous difference between the speeds of light and sound. Information carried by a rapidly moving light wave can be transferred to much slower sound waves, where it is temporarily retained, and then converted back into light.

Because the frozen LiCOF enables such efficient interaction between light and sound, the technology could provide new ways to sharply reduce the amount of energy required by future photonic computing systems.

A New Platform for Photonic and Quantum Technology

The work builds on a long-standing collaboration with Prof. Markus Schmidt and Prof. Mario Chemnitz from the IPHT Jena, who pioneered research involving liquid core optical fibers. Adding the freezing step allowed the researchers to achieve much greater nonlinear effects inside the fiber.

"By freezing the liquid core, we have created an entirely new physical platform that provides extreme nonlinearities while being easy to handle," says Stiller. "While demonstrating a highly efficient optoacoustic memory is a fantastic first step, this level of light-sound coupling not only opens up exciting new possibilities for neuromorphic computing, but also for quantum information processing, microwave photonics and high-precision sensing."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough where freezing the liquid core of optical fibers enhances light-sound interaction by over 1,000 times, enabling optoacoustic memory. This advancement has broad implications for energy-efficient photonic computing and quantum technologies, representing a meaningful technological innovation with potential large-scale benefits.
articles.personality_title: Freezing optical fibers boosts light and sound interaction by 1,000 times
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Optical fibers are thin glass threads that carry light to send information quickly over long distances. Some special fibers have liquid inside their core, which helps with different experiments and technologies.

**What happened** – Scientists from Germany cooled the liquid inside these fibers to very low temperatures, around -196 °C, turning the liquid into a solid. Even when frozen, the fiber still carried light and sound waves. This freezing made light and sound interact more than 1,000 times stronger than usual.

**Impact** – This strong interaction allowed the team to create a kind of memory called optoacoustic memory, where information can be stored temporarily in sound waves inside the fiber. This discovery could help build computers that use light instead of electricity, using much less energy. It also may improve future quantum technologies and sensors.

**What's next step** – Researchers plan to use this frozen fiber technology to develop new types of computers and devices that work faster and need less power. They also want to explore how it can improve quantum information and precise measurements.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Freezing the liquid core of optical fibers creates a powerful new way for light and sound to work together, opening doors to energy-saving photonic computers and advanced technologies.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le gel des fibres optiques multiplie par 1 000 l’interaction lumière-son
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les fibres optiques sont de fins fils de verre qui transportent la lumière pour transmettre rapidement des informations. Certaines fibres spéciales contiennent un liquide dans leur cœur, ce qui aide pour différentes expériences et technologies.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des scientifiques allemands ont refroidi le liquide à l’intérieur de ces fibres à environ -196 °C, transformant le liquide en solide. Même gelée, la fibre conduisait toujours la lumière et les ondes sonores. Ce gel a rendu l’interaction entre la lumière et le son plus de 1 000 fois plus forte que d’habitude.

**Impact** – Cette interaction forte a permis à l’équipe de créer une sorte de mémoire appelée mémoire optoacoustique, où l’information peut être stockée temporairement dans des ondes sonores à l’intérieur de la fibre. Cette découverte pourrait aider à construire des ordinateurs utilisant la lumière au lieu de l’électricité, consommant beaucoup moins d’énergie. Elle pourrait aussi améliorer les technologies quantiques et les capteurs.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent utiliser cette technologie de fibres gelées pour développer de nouveaux types d’ordinateurs et d’appareils plus rapides et moins énergivores. Ils souhaitent aussi explorer ses applications dans l’information quantique et les mesures précises.

**Une phrase clé** – Le gel du cœur liquide des fibres optiques crée un nouveau moyen puissant pour la lumière et le son de travailler ensemble, ouvrant la voie à des ordinateurs photoniques économes en énergie et à des technologies avancées.
articles.personality_title_es: La congelación de fibras ópticas aumenta 1.000 veces la interacción luz-sonido
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las fibras ópticas son hilos muy delgados de vidrio que transportan luz para enviar información rápidamente. Algunas fibras especiales tienen un líquido en su núcleo, lo que ayuda en diferentes experimentos y tecnologías.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos en Alemania enfriaron el líquido dentro de estas fibras a unos -196 °C, convirtiendo el líquido en sólido. Aun estando congelada, la fibra seguía transmitiendo luz y ondas sonoras. Esta congelación hizo que la interacción entre la luz y el sonido fuera más de 1.000 veces más fuerte de lo normal.

**Impacto** – Esta fuerte interacción permitió al equipo crear un tipo de memoria llamada memoria optoacústica, donde la información puede guardarse temporalmente en ondas sonoras dentro de la fibra. Este descubrimiento podría ayudar a construir computadoras que usan luz en lugar de electricidad, con mucho menos consumo de energía. También puede mejorar las tecnologías cuánticas y los sensores.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores planean usar esta tecnología de fibras congeladas para desarrollar nuevos tipos de computadoras y dispositivos que funcionen más rápido y consuman menos energía. También quieren explorar cómo puede mejorar la información cuántica y las mediciones precisas.

**Una frase clave** – Congelar el núcleo líquido de las fibras ópticas crea una nueva forma potente para que la luz y el sonido trabajen juntos, abriendo camino a computadoras fotónicas que ahorran energía y tecnologías avanzadas.
